questions.question: Q: Describe the full heat treatment process for hardening and tempering a high-carbon steel chisel.
questions.correctAnswer: Heat the chisel to above its critical temperature (approximately 800 degrees C) until cherry red. Quench rapidly in oil or water to produce hard martensite. Reheat to approximately 250-300 degrees C (tempering temperature) and hold, then air-cool. This reduces brittleness while maintaining sufficient hardness for cutting.

questions.question: Q: Explain why temperpering is always carried out after hardening.
questions.correctAnswer: Hardening produces a very hard but brittle martensitic structure that is prone to cracking under impact. Tempering reheats to a moderate temperature to allow some carbon to precipitate from the martensite, reducing internal stresses and brittleness while retaining most of the hardness.

questions.question: Q: How does galvanising protect steel from corrosion even if the zinc coating is scratched?
questions.correctAnswer: Zinc is more electrochemically active than steel, so it acts as a sacrificial anode. Even when scratched, the surrounding zinc corrodes preferentially (sacrificial protection), protecting the exposed steel from rusting.

questions.question: Q: Explain the process of electroplating a steel component with chromium.
questions.correctAnswer: The steel component (cathode) and a chromium anode are immersed in a chromium electrolyte solution. A DC current is passed: chromium ions migrate to the cathode and deposit as a thin, hard, corrosion-resistant layer on the component. The current density and time control the plating thickness.

questions.question: Q: Why is normalising carried out after welding a steel component?
questions.correctAnswer: Welding creates a HAZ with uneven grain structure and residual thermal stresses. Normalising heats the component above its critical temperature and air-cools it, producing a uniform fine grain structure and relieving internal stresses throughout the material.
